Q: How to handle data which seems like a duplicate but actually is not A:

To decide if something is a duplicate or not, decide what your primary key actually is.

Your table seems to be about orders. Customer name is not sufficient as a primary key for that. What makes an order unique in your data? Do you have an OrderID? Can one person order the same item multiple times? Why are there even duplicates in the data? If you know where they come from, it may be easier to remove them in a correct way. Probably customer_id, datetime is an acceptable primary key for analyzising such data.

Q: Mainframe modernization vs replatforming: which is better for enterprise systems? A:

Replatforming is usually better when the COBOL application is stable and the main goal is reducing infrastructure cost or moving off the mainframe with minimal risk.

Full modernization makes more sense when you need cloud-native scalability, APIs, faster development, or major architectural improvements.

A practical approach is often replatform first, then modernize critical components gradually. This reduces migration risk while still allowing long-term modernization.

Q: Langchain-community is deprecated or sunset, how to adjust to this? A:

The langchain-community package has been officially sunset and archived as read-only. To adjust, you must migrate your codebase away from it by replacing legacy utilities with dedicated partner packages (like langchain-openai or langchain-anthropic), writing direct custom API wrappers, or isolating orchestration logic behind internal adapters.

The warning appears because the langchain-community repository has been officially archived and frozen by the LangChain team. While it will continue to run for the time being, it will no longer receive security patches, bug fixes, or updates.

Q: How do I use multiple SSH keys on GitHub? A:

If you can keep repositories that are accessed by different SSH keys in different folders, you can follow the steps below:

  1. Generate SSH keys for each identity (work and home) by running the following commands in your terminal:
ssh-keygen -t rsa -C "andrei@work.com"  # Put into default file ~/.ssh/id_rsa
ssh-keygen -t rsa -C "andrei@home.com"  # Put into ~/.ssh/home

  1. Keep your work projects in the folder <..>/projects/work/.

  2. Create SSH configuration file ~/.ssh/config:

Match host github.com exec "[[ $PWD == *projects/work* ]]"
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa

Match host github.com exec "[[ $PWD != *projects/work* ]]"
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/home

The Match host github.com exec "[[ $PWD == *projects/work* ]]" section specifies that when you are in a directory that contains "projects/work" in its path, use the ~/.ssh/id_rsa SSH key.

In all other folders like projects/fun git will use for github.com the SSH key ~/.ssh/home.

So you can use git clone even in not git folder (like in projects/work).

Edit: It's important to make the match patterns mutually exclusive; otherwise, git clone can still authenticate using the wrong key.

Q: Why is my website slow from India to a US GoDaddy server despite low ping? A:

Ping only measures ICMP round-trip latency, so it does not represent the full time required for an HTTPS request. Your results suggest that the main delays are occurring after the basic network connection is established.

In particular, the TLS handshake taking around 0.8–1.4 seconds is worth investigating separately. I would test the site from several locations and compare DNS, TCP connect, TLS, and TTFB times. Also try repeated requests to see whether the delay is consistent.

The TTFB of 1.8–2.3 seconds could be coming from the web server or application rather than the network. For an ASP.NET application, database queries, external API calls, application initialization, server-side processing, or limited hosting resources could all contribute.

I would also compare a static file with the dynamic homepage. If the static file has a low TTFB but the homepage is slow, that points more strongly toward application/server processing. Testing the origin directly versus through any CDN/WAF would also help isolate where the delay is introduced.

So I would not use the ping result alone to judge the site's HTTPS performance. Breaking the request into DNS, TCP, TLS, TTFB, and download phases, as you have already started doing, is the right approach for identifying the bottleneck.
